rounds.proof_sketch: N=2048, TILE_SIZE=32. gridDim.x=(2048+31)/32=64. blockIdx.x∈[0,63], threadIdx.x∈[0,31]. col=blockIdx.x*32+threadIdx.x. col_max=63*32+31=2047. Since col_max=2047<N=2048, the condition col==N is NEVER reachable. Both 'col<N' and 'col<=N' evaluate identically for all col∈[0,2047].
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation changes the write-back guard from 'col < N' to 'col <= N', which would only produce different behavior when col equals N (2048). However, with the fixed dimensions (N=2048, TILE_SIZE=32), the grid is launched with exactly 64 blocks in the x-direction. The maximum column index any thread can compute is (gridDim.x-1)*TILE_SIZE+(TILE_SIZE-1) = 63*32+31 = 2047. Since col can never reach 2048, the boundary case that would distinguish the mutant is mathematically unreachable. This is a classic case where the grid dimension calculation perfectly covers N without overflow, making the boundary guard relaxation semantically invisible.
rounds.kill_strategy: This mutant is truly unkillable under the fixed-shape contract. The mutation would only matter if N were NOT a multiple of TILE_SIZE (32), which would cause some threads to have col values >= N. But N=2048 is exactly divisible by 32, so the grid perfectly tiles the output with no thread ever having col=N. Changing the shape would be required to kill this mutant, which violates the contract.
rounds.recommendations: For mutation testing of tiled GPU kernels, explicitly test with dimensions that are NOT multiples of the tile size. The current fixed shape (N=2048=64*32) creates an 'accidentally equivalent' mutant because the grid exactly covers the output without boundary spillover. Adding test configurations where N%TILE_SIZE≠0 would catch such boundary-condition mutations.
